source.author: verg
source.text: Dixerat Anchises, natumque unaque Sibyllam conventus trahit in medios turbamque sonantem, et tumulum capit, unde omnes longo ordine possit adversos legere, et venientum discere vultus.
source.text_original: Dixerat Anchises, natumque unaque Sibyllam / conventus trahit in medios turbamque sonantem, / et tumulum capit, unde omnes longo ordine possit / adversos legere, et venientum discere vultus.
source.text_english: Anchises had spoken, and he leads his son and the Sibyl together into the middle of the assembly and to a roaring crowd, and he takes a mound from which he can read all those facing him in a long line and learn the faces of those who are coming.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: hic et Naubolides tortas consurgit in undas Iphitus, hic patrium frangit Neptunius aequor qui tenet undisonam Psamathen semperque patentem Taenaron Euphemus, mollique a litore Pellae Deucalion certus iaculis et comminus ense nobilis Amphion, pariter quos edidit Hypso nec potuit similes voluitve ediscere vultus.
reuse.text_original: hic et Naubolides tortas consurgit in undas / Iphitus, hic patrium frangit Neptunius aequor / qui tenet undisonam Psamathen semperque patentem / Taenaron Euphemus, mollique a litore Pellae / Deucalion certus iaculis et comminus ense / nobilis Amphion, pariter quos edidit Hypso / nec potuit similes voluitve ediscere vultus.
reuse.text_english: Here too rises Iphitus, son of Naubolus, into the twisting waves; here Euphemus, the son of Neptune, who holds Psamathe sounding with waves and ever-open Taenarum, breaks his native sea; Deucalion from the soft shore of Pella, renowned for spears and also for the sword at close quarters; Amphion, distinguished alike by both weapons, whom Hypso bore and whose like she could not, or would not, learn to shape in face.
